o: Replace 0s with distinct even positive integers and 1s with distinct odd positive integers so that each array is strictly increasing, all integers across both arrays are distinct, and the maximum value used is minimized. Crucially, if we assign numbers in increasing global order, each array automatically receives an increasing subsequence — so a valid assignment is exactly a shuffle (interleaving) of the two bit-patterns whose parity sequence matches the parities of the chosen numbers. Example 2 shows counts alone are insufficient: with 4 zeros and 4 ones, M=8 fails structurally and the answer is 9.
k: Feasibility for a cap M is monotone: any assignment valid for M works for M+1, enabling binary search on the answer.
Feasibility check: does some shuffle of nums1 and nums2 match a subsequence of the parity string of 1..M? Solve with DP f(i, j) = earliest consumed position, using precomputed next-occurrence tables.
Answer bounds: at least L = |nums1| + |nums2| numbers are needed; doubling the search ceiling until feasible keeps the search safe.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear Scan over M with DP Check (Intuitive)
a.i: Try M = L, L+1, ... and test each with the shuffle-matching DP; return the first feasible M. Simple to reason about but the repeated O(L²) checks make it slow for large answers; it mainly establishes the feasibility criterion before we binary-search it.
s: Define parity string P(t) = t mod 2 for t = 1..M and next-occurrence table nxt[p][t].
DP f(i, j): earliest position reachable after shuffling prefixes of nums1 (i items) and nums2 (j items).
Transition: f(i+1, j) = min(..., nxt[bit][f(i,j)+1]) and symmetrically for j.
Increase M until f(L1, L2) is reachable; return that M.
a.t: O(A · L²) where A is the answer gap — potentially slow, motivates binary search
a.sp: O(L²) for the DP table plus O(M) for next-occurrence tables

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on the Answer (Optimal)
a.i: Because feasibility is monotone in M, binary search replaces the linear scan. Start with lo = L (need L distinct numbers) and a safely large hi (double it until feasible). Each check is the same O(L²) shuffle-matching DP, so the total is O(L² log L) — about 4e7 lightweight steps for L = 2000.
s: Set lo = L1 + L2 and hi = 2·lo; while not feasible(hi), double hi.
Binary search the smallest M with feasible(M) using the DP check from Approach 1.
a.t: O(L² log L) — about 20 binary-search iterations of an O(L²) DP for L = 2000
a.sp: O(L²) for the DP table plus O(M) for next-occurrence tables

w: The crucial insight is the shuffle characterization: increasing global assignment order makes per-array monotonicity free, leaving only a parity-sequence matching problem. Edge cases: nums1 may be empty (then the answer tracks nums2's pattern alone); all-zeros needs the L-th even = 2L. Verify example 2 returns 9, not 8 — pure counting is a trap. Follow-up: reconstruct the actual arrays by storing DP choices.
